title: Exora Astrophysics Academy
subtitle: Comprehensive Guide to Exoplanetary Detection, Habitability Modeling, and Astrobiology

sections.title: Exoplanet Fundamentals
sections.description: Understanding how astronomers discover and classify alien worlds beyond our solar system.

accordions.question: Tired of Earth? Here's your exit list.
points: -> Exoplanets are planets orbiting stars outside our Solar System.
-> Over 5,600 exoplanets have been confirmed by NASA missions like Kepler, TESS, and Spitzer.
-> Detection techniques include Transit Photometry (brightness dips) and Radial Velocity (stellar wobble).
accordions.summary: Understanding the exoplanetary catalog begins by observing how planets periodically occlude stellar light and induce gravitational perturbations on their host star.

accordions.question: How do we measure exoplanet size and mass?
points: -> Transit depth (ΔF/F) directly measures the planet-to-star area ratio (R_p / R_*)^2.
-> Radial velocity amplitude measures gravitational wobble to derive minimum planetary mass (m sin i).
-> Combining radius and mass gives bulk density, confirming whether a world is rocky like Earth or gas-dominated like Neptune.
accordions.summary: Mass and radius together reveal bulk density, distinguishing rocky terrestrial worlds from Hycean ocean worlds and mini-Neptunes.

sections.title: Circumstellar Habitable Zone (HZ)
sections.description: The thermal orbital boundary where liquid water can persist on a terrestrial planet surface.

accordions.question: Goldilocks Zone — unlocked.
points: -> The Circumstellar Habitable Zone (HZ) is the orbital distance where surface liquid water can exist.
-> Hotter G/F-type stars push the HZ outward (1.0 - 2.5 AU); cooler M-dwarfs pull the HZ close (0.01 - 0.2 AU).
-> Being in the HZ is a prerequisite, but atmosphere and magnetic fields are required for liquid surface oceans.
accordions.summary: Liquid surface water requires a precise thermodynamic balance between stellar irradiance flux and atmospheric greenhouse trapping.

accordions.question: What is the Earth Similarity Index (ESI)?
points: -> ESI is a normalized scale from 0.0 (no similarity) to 1.00 (identical to Earth).
-> Evaluated using Schulze-Makuch (2011) geometric weighted mean across radius, density, and temperature.
-> Planets with ESI > 0.80 are prime candidates for terrestrial surface environments.
accordions.summary: ESI allows planetary scientists to algorithmically screen thousands of cataloged worlds for Earth-like physical parameters.

sections.title: Astrobiology & Atmospheric Biosignatures
sections.description: How spectroscopy detects chemical atmospheric disequilibrium and potential biological signatures.

accordions.question: Okay but can we ACTUALLY know if a planet supports life?
points: -> Transmission spectroscopy analyzes starlight filtered through a planet's atmospheric limb during transit.
-> Biosignatures include atmospheric disequilibrium—such as simultaneous oxygen (O2/O3) and methane (CH4).
-> JWST is actively characterizing atmospheric absorption lines on targets like TRAPPIST-1e and K2-18b.
accordions.summary: Direct spectrographic identification of gas disequilibrium provides our most concrete pathway to detecting extraterrestrial biospheres.
